subQuestions.questionText: Several forces are acting on a moving object. Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT when these forces are in equilibrium?

options.A: The velocity of the object is increasing.
options.B: The object is moving at a constant velocity.
options.C: The kinetic energy of the object is decreasing.
options.D: The object has a non-zero acceleration.

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (2 marks)
When the net (resultant) force is zero the object is in equilibrium, so it moves at constant velocity (zero acceleration).

subQuestions.questionText: A stone thrown vertically downwards from the top of a building takes t seconds to strike the ground. Consider the acceleration-time graph for the motion of the stone: acceleration is constant at 9,8 m·s⁻² from time 0 to time t, and the shaded area lies between this line and the time axis from 0 to t. The effects of air friction are ignored. What does the shaded area between 0 and t seconds, shown in the graph, represent? *(Refer to the acceleration-time graph in the original question paper.)*

options.A: The final velocity of the stone
options.B: The change in position of the stone
options.C: The constant velocity of the stone
options.D: The change in velocity of the stone

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
The area under an acceleration-time graph (a × t) gives the change in velocity of the stone.

subQuestions.questionText: A ball moving horizontally has constant momentum p and kinetic energy K. The ball collides with a wall and bounces back horizontally. Immediately after the collision, the ball has momentum ½p (in the opposite direction). The mass of the ball remains constant. Which ONE of the following is the kinetic energy of the ball immediately after the collision? *(Refer to the diagram of the ball and wall in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (2 marks)
Since K = p²/(2m) and mass is constant, K ∝ p². Halving the momentum (p → ½p) reduces the kinetic energy to (½)² = ¼ of the original, i.e. ¼K.

subQuestions.questionText: A force F acts on a box as the box moves from rest down a rough incline at a constant acceleration. The force F is parallel to the incline and directed up the incline (opposing the motion). Choose the option that CORRECTLY completes the following statement. The work done by the gravitational force is ... the work done by the frictional force and the work done by F. *(Refer to the diagram of the box on the incline in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (2 marks)
The box accelerates down the incline, so the net work is positive (Wnet = ΔK > 0). Since Wnet = Wgravity − (Wfriction + WF magnitudes opposing motion), the work done by gravity must be greater than the sum of the work done by friction and by F.

subQuestions.questionText: A ball falling vertically downwards from point A strikes the ground with velocity v and bounces, reaching a maximum height at point B (B lower than A). Which ONE of the combinations below is CORRECT for the direction of the impulse on the ball upon striking the ground and the magnitude of the velocity with which the ball leaves the ground? *(Refer to the diagram of the bouncing ball in the original question paper.)*

options.A: Direction of impulse: Upward; Magnitude of velocity leaving ground: Greater than v
options.B: Direction of impulse: Downward; Magnitude of velocity leaving ground: Greater than v
options.C: Direction of impulse: Upward; Magnitude of velocity leaving ground: Less than v
options.D: Direction of impulse: Downward; Magnitude of velocity leaving ground: Less than v

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (2 marks)
The impulse (change in momentum) is directed upward. Since the ball rises to a height lower than A, it leaves the ground with a velocity of magnitude less than v.

subQuestions.questionText: The absorption spectrum of an element surrounding a moving star is observed on Earth and found to be red shifted. Which ONE of the following combinations is CORRECT for the movement of the star and the frequency of the observed light on Earth?

options.A: Movement of star: Away from Earth; Frequency of observed light on Earth: Decreased
options.B: Movement of star: Towards Earth; Frequency of observed light on Earth: Decreased
options.C: Movement of star: Away from Earth; Frequency of observed light on Earth: Increased
options.D: Movement of star: Towards Earth; Frequency of observed light on Earth: Increased

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (2 marks)
A red shift means the observed wavelength increases and the frequency decreases, which occurs when the star is moving away from Earth.

subQuestions.questionText: Two small identical spheres, each with mass m and charge +Q, are placed in a vertical cylinder. The spheres remain stationary when their centres are r metres apart (one sphere resting above the other), as shown in the diagram. Ignore ALL frictional effects. Which ONE of the following expressions can be used to CORRECTLY calculate the distance r? *(Refer to the diagram of the spheres in the cylinder in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (2 marks)
The upper sphere is in equilibrium: the electrostatic repulsion balances its weight, kQ²/r² = mg. Solving for r gives r = √(kQ²/mg).

subQuestions.questionText: The kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a unit of ...
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (2 marks)
The kilowatt-hour is power (kW) multiplied by time (h), which is a unit of electrical energy.

subQuestions.questionText: The diagram shows a simplified electric motor with a coil between the N and S poles of a magnet. The rotation of the coil is observed from the battery. Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT while the motor is in operation? The coil and the ... *(Refer to the diagram of the electric motor in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
A DC electric motor uses a (split-ring) commutator, not slip rings, and for the arrangement shown the coil and commutator rotate anti-clockwise.

subQuestions.questionText: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for the photoelectric effect? The photoelectric effect demonstrates that: (i) Light has a wave nature; (ii) Light has a particle nature; (iii) Light energy is quantised.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
The photoelectric effect demonstrates that light behaves as particles (photons) and that light energy is quantised, i.e. statements (ii) and (iii).

subQuestions.questionText: In an experiment, a crate of mass 8,5 kg, lying stationary on a rough horizontal table, is connected to a mass hanger by means of a light inextensible string passing over a frictionless pulley. Mass pieces are added to the mass hanger and the acceleration of the crate is measured. The experiment is repeated several times by adding different masses to increase the hanging mass each time. Ignore the effects of air friction. The results were used to draw a sketch graph of the acceleration of the crate (m·s⁻²) versus the hanging mass (kg); the graph has a value Y on the acceleration axis and shows hanging-mass values of 4,2 kg and 7,4 kg on the horizontal axis. Define the term static friction. *(Refer to the apparatus diagram and acceleration vs hanging-mass graph in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Marking criteria (2 marks): If any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.
The force that opposes the tendency of motion of a stationary object relative/parallel to a surface.

subQuestions.questionText: Draw a labelled free-body diagram showing ALL the HORIZONTAL forces acting on the crate JUST BEFORE it starts moving.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Horizontal forces on the crate: fs (static friction) acting in one direction and T (tension) acting in the opposite direction.
Accepted labels: fs = static friction / f / Ff / Fw (Afrikaans only); T = FT / Fstring / tension / Ftou.
Notes: Do not penalise if vertical forces (w, N) are shown. Mark awarded for label and arrow. Do not penalise for length of arrows. If arrows do not touch the dot: Max 1/2. Any other additional force(s) except w and N: Max 1/2. If everything correct but no arrows: Max 1/2.

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the coefficient of static friction (μs). (The crate begins to move when the hanging mass is 4,2 kg; the crate has mass 8,5 kg. Use g = 9,8 m·s⁻².)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
For hanging mass (at the point of motion): Fnet = ma; mg − T = 0, so T = mg = 4,2(9,8) = 41,16 N ✓ (formula) ✓ (substitution)
For crate (just before moving): T − fs(max) = 0, so fs(max) = T and fs(max) = μsN.
μs(8,5)(9,8) = 41,16 ✓
μs = 0,49 ✓
Alternative: fs(max) = μs·mcrate·g = mhanging·g → μs(8,5)(9,8) = 4,2(9,8) → μs(8,5) = 4,2 → μs = 0,49 ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration represented by Y on the graph if the coefficient of kinetic friction between the crate and the table is 0,40. (At Y the hanging mass is 7,4 kg and the crate mass is 8,5 kg.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
For crate: Fnet = ma; T − fk = ma → T − μk·mg = ma
T − 0,4(8,5)(9,8) = 8,5a ......... Eqn (1) ✓ (formula) ✓ (substitution)
For hanging mass: Fnet = ma; mg − T = ma
7,4(9,8) − T = 7,4a ......... Eqn (2) ✓ (substitution)
Solving simultaneously: Y = a = 2,47 m·s⁻² ✓ ✓
NOTE: T can be calculated first (54,32 N).

subQuestions.questionText: A 5 kg block is now placed inside the crate and the experiment is repeated. How will this affect the maximum static frictional force now experienced by the crate? Choose from INCREASES, DECREASES or REMAINS THE SAME. Give a reason for the answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
INCREASES ✓
Reason: fs(max) ∝ N OR fs(max) ∝ m OR fs(max) = μsN OR the normal force acting on the crate increases OR increase in mass/weight of crate increases the normal force. ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Ball A is thrown vertically upwards at 12 m·s⁻¹ from the top of a building. Two seconds after ball A was thrown upwards, ball B is thrown vertically downwards at 5,4 m·s⁻¹ from the top of the same building. Both balls, A and B, strike the ground at time t seconds. Ignore the effects of air friction. The position-time sketch graphs for both balls are shown (ball A rising to a peak at Y before falling, ball B starting later at position Z on the A curve). Using EQUATIONS OF MOTION ONLY, calculate the value of t as shown in the graphs. *(Refer to the position-time graph in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
• Formula y = viΔt + ½aΔt² ✓
• Correct substitution for ball A ✓
• Correct substitution for ball B ✓
• yA = yB ✓
Final answer: t = 4 s ✓
UPWARDS AS POSITIVE:
Ball A: y = 12t + ½(−9,8)t² ......... Eqn (1)
Ball B: y = −5,4(t − 2) + ½(−9,8)(t − 2)² ......... Eqn (2)
Equating: 12t + ½(−9,8)t² = −5,4(t − 2) + ½(−9,8)(t − 2)² → t = 4 s ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Using EQUATIONS OF MOTION ONLY, calculate the value of Z as shown in the graphs. (Z is the position, measured from the top of the building, of ball B at the moment it is thrown, i.e. the position of ball A at t = 2 s below the top of the building.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
• Correct formula ✓
• Correct substitution ✓
• Correct final answer: 30,4 m ✓
UPWARDS AS POSITIVE, using ball A at t = 4 s and comparing, or ball B:
Ball A: y = viΔt + ½aΔt² = (12)(4) + ½(−9,8)(4)² = −30,4 m → Z = 30,4 m ✓
OR Ball B: y = (−5,4)(4 − 2) + ½(−9,8)(4 − 2)² = −30,4 m → Z = 30,4 m

subQuestions.questionText: Using EQUATIONS OF MOTION ONLY, calculate the value of Y as shown in the graphs. (Y is the maximum height reached by ball A above the ground, i.e. the maximum height above the top of the building plus the total drop.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks) — POSITIVE MARKING FROM 3.1.1 and 3.1.2:
• Correct equation to calculate y ✓
• Correct substitution to calculate y ✓
• Adding 30,4 to y ✓
• Correct final answer: 37,75 m ✓ (Range: 37,72 – 37,75 m)
UPWARDS AS POSITIVE:
Ball A: vf² = vi² + 2ay; 0 = (12)² + 2(−9,8)y → y = 7,35 m
Y = 7,35 + 30,4 = 37,75 m ✓
Note: vf and vi can be interchanged.

subQuestions.questionText: On the same set of axes, sketch the velocity-time graphs for ball A and ball B while they are in free fall. Label the graphs A and B for ball A and ball B respectively. Clearly indicate the following on the graphs: the initial velocity of each ball; the time at which each ball is thrown; the time at which the balls strike the ground.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks) — POSITIVE MARKING FROM 3.1.1:
• Correct initial velocities of both balls A and B with correct shape (straight lines with both positive / both negative slopes) ✓
• Correct initial times for balls A and B, with B starting after the intercept of A ✓
• Both graphs end at 4 s (accept t) ✓
• Graphs parallel to each other and B to the right of A ✓
(Taking upwards as positive: line A starts at +12 m·s⁻¹ at t = 0; line B starts at −5,4 m·s⁻¹ at t = 2 s; both lines have the same negative slope (−9,8) and both reach the ground at t = 4 s.)
NB: If no labels A and B, deduct 1 mark.

subQuestions.questionText: Two trolleys, A and B, of masses 1,5 kg and 2 kg respectively, are held stationary on a straight, horizontal, frictionless track, with a compressed spring between them. The trolleys are released and the spring takes t seconds to return to its natural length, then falls to the ground. Trolley A moves to the left, while trolley B moves to the right and then up a frictionless inclined plane, rising to a maximum vertical height of 1,5 m. Ignore the rotational effects of the wheels. Write down the principle of conservation of mechanical energy in words. *(Refer to the before/after diagram of the trolleys and spring in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Marking criteria (2 marks): If any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.
The total mechanical energy / sum of gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy, in an isolated system remains constant / is conserved.

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the speed of trolley B at the bottom of the inclined plane. (Trolley B rises to a maximum vertical height of 1,5 m on a frictionless incline; use g = 9,8 m·s⁻².)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Using conservation of mechanical energy:
(Ep + Ek)top = (Ep + Ek)bottom
(mgh + ½mv²)top = (mgh + ½mv²)bottom
(2)(9,8)(1,5) + 0 = 0 + ½(2)v² ✓ ✓ ✓
v = 5,42 m·s⁻¹ ✓
(OR (9,8)(1,5) + 0 = 0 + ½v²)

subQuestions.questionText: For the t seconds that the spring takes to return to its natural length, calculate the change in momentum of trolley B. (Trolley B has mass 2 kg and leaves the spring at the speed found in 4.2.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks) — POSITIVE MARKING FROM 4.2:
Δp = mvf − mvi ✓ (formula)
= 2(5,42 − 0) ✓ (substitution)
= 10,84 kg·m·s⁻¹ to the right ✓
(OR 2(−5,42 − 0) = −10,84 kg·m·s⁻¹)

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the change in momentum of trolley A.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark) — POSITIVE MARKING FROM 4.3.1:
10,84 kg·m·s⁻¹ to the left / opposite direction ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the speed of trolley A after t seconds. (Trolley A has mass 1,5 kg.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks) — POSITIVE MARKING FROM 4.2 and 4.3.1:
ΔpA = mvf − mvi
−10,84 = 1,5(vf − 0) → vf = −7,23 m·s⁻¹ ✓
speed v = 7,23 m·s⁻¹ ✓
(OR by conservation of momentum: 0 = 1,5vf + (2)(5,42) → vf = −7,23 m·s⁻¹; v = 7,23 m·s⁻¹)

subQuestions.questionText: A constant force F is applied at an angle of 30° to the horizontal on a crate of mass 6 kg that is initially at rest. A constant frictional force of 10 N acts on the crate as it moves from rest at point A along a horizontal surface to point B. The distance between A and B is 1,5 m. The speed of the crate at B is 2 m·s⁻¹. Define the term work done by a force. *(Refer to the diagram of the crate and applied force F in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Marking criteria (2 marks): If any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.
The work done on an object by a constant force F is FΔxcosθ, where F is the magnitude of the force, Δx the magnitude of the displacement and θ the angle between the force and the displacement.
OR The work done on an object is the product of the force and the displacement of the object in the direction of the displacement.

subQuestions.questionText: Draw a labelled free-body diagram showing ALL the forces acting on the crate as it moves.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Forces on the crate: N (normal force, up), F (applied force at 30° above horizontal), f (friction, opposing motion) and w (weight, down). ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓
Accepted labels: w = Fw / Fg / mg / 58,8 N / gravitational force / weight; f = Ff / fk / (kinetic) friction; N = FN / normal force; F = FA / applied force.
Notes: Mark awarded for label and arrow. Do not penalise for length of arrows. Any other additional force(s): Max 3/4. If everything correct but no arrows: Max 3/4. If force(s) do not make contact with the dot: Max 3/4. If components drawn for F: Max 3/4.

subQuestions.questionText: Using ENERGY PRINCIPLES ONLY, calculate the magnitude of force F.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
• Correct formula for Wnet / Wnc ✓
• Correct substitution for work done by the forces ✓
• Correct substitution for change in kinetic (and potential) energy ✓
• Correct final answer: 20,79 N ✓ (Range: 20,769 – 20,79 N)
Using the work-energy theorem (horizontal surface, ΔEp = 0):
WF + Wf = ΔEk → FΔxcosθ + fΔxcos180° = ½mvf² − ½mvi²
F(1,5)cos30° + 10(1,5)cos180° = ½(6)(2² − 0²)
F = 20,78 N ✓

subQuestions.questionText: A 2 kg object is placed in the crate. What effect will this have on the work done by the same force F when the crate is again moved from point A to point B? Write only INCREASES, DECREASES or REMAINS THE SAME.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
REMAINS THE SAME ✓✓
(The work done by F = FΔxcosθ depends only on F, the displacement and the angle, none of which change.)

subQuestions.questionText: A stationary listener, standing on the roadside, records the wavelength of the sound emitted by the siren of a police car travelling at a constant velocity. In the wavelength-time graph (not drawn to scale), L is the wavelength of the sound recorded by the listener (0,40 m) and S is the wavelength of the sound emitted by the siren (0,38 m). Take the speed of sound in air to be 343 m·s⁻¹. Name the phenomenon that explains why the wavelengths shown in the graph differ. *(Refer to the wavelength-time graph in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Doppler Effect ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Is the car moving TOWARDS or AWAY FROM the listener? Give a reason for the answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Away from ✓
Reason: The wavelength of sound detected/observed by the listener is longer than the wavelength emitted by the source (L > S) OR the frequency detected by the listener is lower than the frequency of the source (fL < fs). ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the frequency of the sound emitted by the siren. (Wavelength emitted by siren, S = 0,38 m; speed of sound = 343 m·s⁻¹.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
v = fλ ✓
343 = f(0,38) ✓
f = 902,63 Hz ✓
(If c = fλ used, penalise 1 mark. If 340 used, penalise 1 mark for answer.)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the magnitude of the velocity of the car. (Wavelength detected by listener, L = 0,40 m; speed of sound = 343 m·s⁻¹.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (6 marks) — POSITIVE MARKING FROM 6.3.1:
First find the frequency detected by the listener:
v = fλ → 343 = fL(0,40) → fL = 857,5 Hz ✓ ✓ ✓
Apply the Doppler equation (source receding):
fL = [v / (v + vs)]·fs
857,5 = [343 / (343 + vs)](902,63) ✓ ✓
vs = 18,05 m·s⁻¹ ✓ (Range: 18,05 m·s⁻¹ to 18,45 m·s⁻¹)
If wavelengths are substituted instead of frequencies: max 2/6. If wavelengths are swopped: max 3/6.

subQuestions.questionText: P is a +2 nC point charge. X is a point 6 cm away from charge P. Calculate the magnitude of the electric field at X. *(Refer to the diagram of charge P and point X in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
E = kQ/r² ✓
= (9×10⁹)(2×10⁻⁹) / (0,06)² ✓
= 5×10³ N·C⁻¹ (5 000 N·C⁻¹) ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Point charge S, with a charge of −2 nC, is placed 4 cm to the right of charge P (+2 nC). Draw the resultant electric field pattern due to charges P and S. *(Refer to the diagram of charges P and S in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Criteria for sketch (field pattern of two unlike/opposite charges, a dipole):
• Correct direction of field lines (from +P to −S) ✓
• Correct shape of the electric field lines between the charges and on the outside of the charges ✓
• No field lines crossing each other; field lines must touch the charge but not go inside the charge ✓
Note: If learner draws field pattern of two like charges: 0/3. If only one charge is drawn: 0/3.

subQuestions.questionText: A third point charge T is placed 2 cm to the right of S (so P is at the left, S is 4 cm to the right of P, and T is a further 2 cm to the right of S). Point charge T experiences a net electrostatic force of 2,5 × 10⁻⁴ N to the left. State Coulomb's law in words. *(Refer to the diagram of charges P, S and T in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Marking criteria (2 marks): If any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.
The magnitude of the electrostatic force exerted by one point charge on another point charge is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
NOTE: If reference to masses / if the word FORCE in context omitted: 0/2.

subQuestions.questionText: What is the polarity of charge T? Choose from POSITIVE or NEGATIVE.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
POSITIVE ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the magnitude of charge T. (T is 2 cm from S (−2 nC) and 6 cm from P (+2 nC); the net electrostatic force on T is 2,5 × 10⁻⁴ N to the left.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks) — POSITIVE MARKING FROM 7.1 in terms of conversions:
• Formula for Coulomb's law F = kQ₁Q₂/r² ✓
• Correct substitution for BOTH FST and FPT ✓
• Substitution of 2,5×10⁻⁴ N for Fnet ✓
• Subtraction (FS − FP or FP − FS) ✓
• Correct final answer: 6,25×10⁻⁹ C ✓
FST = (9×10⁹)(2×10⁻⁹)QT / (0,02)²  and  FPT = (9×10⁹)(2×10⁻⁹)QT / (0,06)²
Fnet = FST − FPT:
2,5×10⁻⁴ = [(9×10⁹)(2×10⁻⁹)QT / (0,02)²] − [(9×10⁹)(2×10⁻⁹)QT / (0,06)²]
QT = 6,25×10⁻⁹ C ✓

subQuestions.questionText: L1 and L2 are two light bulbs with the following ratings: L1: 36 W ; 20 V and L2: 48 W ; 32 V. The two bulbs are connected in a circuit. The battery has an internal resistance of 0,6 Ω while the conducting wires and the ammeters have negligible resistance. R1 and R2 are resistors (R2 = 4 Ω). Ammeter A1 reads the total current; ammeter A2 reads the current through the L2 branch; L1 is in series with R1, and this combination is in parallel with L2, with R2 (4 Ω) and the battery in the main circuit. Define the term power. *(Refer to the circuit diagram in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks) — (2 or 0):
The rate at which work is done / dissipated OR energy transferred OR work done per unit time.

subQuestions.questionText: If both light bulbs operate as RATED, calculate the reading on ammeter A2. (A2 reads the current through bulb L2, rated 48 W ; 32 V.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
P = VI ✓
48 = 32 I ✓
I = 1,5 A ✓
(OR using P = V²/R: 48 = 32²/R → R = 21,33 Ω, then I = 1,5 A)

subQuestions.questionText: If both light bulbs operate as RATED, calculate the reading on ammeter A1. (A1 reads the total current; bulb L1 is rated 36 W ; 20 V.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks) — POSITIVE MARKING FROM 8.2.1:
For L1: P = VI → 36 = 20I → I = 1,8 A ✓ ✓
ITOT = 1,5 + 1,8 = 3,3 A ✓

subQuestions.questionText: If both light bulbs operate as RATED, calculate the resistance of resistor R1. (R1 is in series with bulb L1 in the branch that is in parallel with L2, whose potential difference is 32 V.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
The L1 + R1 branch is in parallel with L2, so V across the branch = 32 V.
VR1 + VL1 = V// → VR1 + 20 = 32 → VR1 = 12 V ✓
V = IR → 12 = 1,8 R1 ✓ ✓
R1 = 6,67 Ω ✓
(OR total branch resistance 32 = 1,8R → R = 17,77 Ω; RL1 = 20²/36 = 11,11 Ω; R1 = 17,77 − 11,11 = 6,67 Ω)

subQuestions.questionText: If both light bulbs operate as RATED, calculate the emf of the battery. (R2 = 4 Ω is in series with the parallel combination; internal resistance r = 0,6 Ω; total current 3,3 A.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks) — POSITIVE MARKING FROM 8.2.2 and 8.2.3:
V across R2: V2 = ITOT·R2 = 3,3(4) = 13,2 V ✓
emf = Vext + Ir = (13,2 + 32) + 3,3(0,6) ✓ ✓
= 47,18 V ✓ (Range: 47,16 – 47,19 V)

subQuestions.questionText: Bulb L1 burns out after a while. Assume that the resistance of bulb L2 remains constant. Will bulb L2 continue to glow after bulb L1 burns out? Choose from YES or NO. Support your answer with a suitable calculation.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks) — POSITIVE MARKING FROM 8.2.1 and 8.2.4:
NO / NEE (accept: will not glow) ✓
RL2 = V²/P = 32²/48 = 21,33 Ω (OR RL2 = V/I = 32/1,5 = 21,33 Ω) ✓
emf = I(R + r): 47,18 = I(21,33 + 4 + 0,6) ✓ ✓
I = 1,82 A ✓
(The current through L2 changes from its rated value, so it does not operate as rated / does not glow as before.)
NOTE: If 21,33 Ω already calculated previously, award the mark.

subQuestions.questionText: The graph shows how the induced current in a generator varies with time. The current is always positive, rising from 0 to a peak of 1,2 A and back to 0 in a repeating pattern with a period of 0,02 s (i.e. peaks near 0,01 s and 0,03 s). Name the type of generator. Choose from AC or DC. *(Refer to the induced current vs time graph in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
DC (generator) ✓

subQuestions.questionText: State the energy conversion that takes place in this generator while it is in operation.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks) — (2 or 0):
Mechanical / Kinetic to Electrical (energy). ✓✓

subQuestions.questionText: Give a reason why this generator is NOT suitable for the transmission of electricity over long distances.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Power / energy / voltage loss cannot be reduced / will be too large OR the current cannot be made smaller. ✓
Accept: Transformers do not use DC / DC cannot be stepped up or down.

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the frequency at which the coil rotates in the generator. (The period of the induced current is 0,02 s.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
f = 1/T = 1/0,02 = 50 Hz ✓✓
OR f = number of waves/cycles ÷ time = 2/0,04 = 50 Hz

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term root mean square (rms) current.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marking criteria (2 marks): If any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.
Root-mean-square current is the alternating current that dissipates the same amount of energy as an equivalent DC current.

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the root-mean-square current delivered by the generator. (The maximum induced current is 1,2 A.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Irms = Imax/√2 ✓
= 1,2/√2 ✓
= 0,85 A ✓

subQuestions.questionText: A second graph shows how the induced current varies with time after a change was made to the operation of the generator: the peak current is now 0,6 A and the period is now 0,04 s (peaks near 0,02 s), i.e. both the maximum current and the frequency have changed compared to the original graph. Fully describe the change that was made. *(Refer to the second induced current vs time graph in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
The speed of rotation was halved. ✓✓
Accept: Frequency was halved / period was doubled.
(If only speed of rotation slower / frequency decreases / period increased: 1/2.)

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term photoelectric effect.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marking criteria (2 marks): If any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.
The process whereby electrons are ejected from a metal surface when light (of suitable frequency) is incident/shining on that surface.

subQuestions.questionText: Red light, blue light and green light are shone simultaneously on a sheet of potassium. Each colour of light consists of a single frequency. Two maximum kinetic energies of the ejected electrons are possible, namely 6,96 × 10⁻²⁰ J and 2,65 × 10⁻²⁰ J. Each ejected electron has only one of these maximum kinetic energies. Which colour of light is responsible for ejecting electrons that have a maximum kinetic energy equal to 2,65 × 10⁻²⁰ J? *(Refer to the diagram of the light shining on the potassium sheet in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Green ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the answer to QUESTION 10.2.1.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Only green and blue light eject electrons / red light does not eject electrons. Green has a lower frequency than blue (green has a longer wavelength than blue) / photons of blue light have more energy than photons of green light, and therefore green ejects electrons with the lower kinetic energy. (fgreen < fblue.) ✓✓

subQuestions.questionText: The electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of 2,65 × 10⁻²⁰ J are ejected by light that has a frequency of 5,85 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate the frequency of the light that ejected electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of 6,96 × 10⁻²⁰ J.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
First find the work function using the green light data:
E = W₀ + Ek(max); hf = W₀ + Ek(max)
(6,63×10⁻³⁴)(5,85×10¹⁴) = W₀ + 2,65×10⁻²⁰ ✓ ✓
W₀ = 3,61×10⁻¹⁹ J ✓
Then for the higher-energy electrons:
hf = W₀ + Ek(max)
(6,63×10⁻³⁴)f = 3,61×10⁻¹⁹ + 6,96×10⁻²⁰ ✓
f = 6,5×10¹⁴ Hz ✓
(OR directly: hf₁ − Ek(max)₁ = hf₂ − Ek(max)₂ → f₂ = 6,5×10¹⁴ Hz)

subQuestions.questionText: The intensity of the red light is increased, while the intensities of the blue light and green light remain the same. What effect will this change have on the rate at which electrons are ejected? Choose from INCREASES, DECREASES or REMAINS THE SAME.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Remains the same ✓✓
(Red light does not have a high enough frequency to eject electrons from potassium, so increasing its intensity has no effect on the rate of ejection.)

subQuestions.questionText: Some of the atoms of a hot gas, made up of a single element, are in an excited state. The spectrum formed by the hot gas is observed on a screen in a darkened room. The spectrum consists of specific coloured lines on a black background. Name the type of spectrum formed.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
(Line) emission spectrum ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the presence of the coloured lines in the spectrum.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
The coloured lines represent the (associated) frequencies / wavelengths / energy of the emitted (photons) when atoms / electrons move to a lower energy level. ✓✓
